title: Before We Rush Forward, Let's Remember Why We Began November 10, 2026
author: Kathleen Schafer
source: Extraordinarily Ordinary: A Field Guide for Being Human (kathleenschafer.substack.com),
summary: Schafer, writing to what she calls soulful leaders, uses the moment after an election to argue that newly empowered leaders should reconnect with their original reason for serving before the demands of office take over. She observes that accumulating responsibilities can leave capable people disconnected from what first inspired them. The move is to treat stillness and a humane pace as leadership practices, not luxuries, and to extend the advice from officeholders to anyone who hopes to build something better. She uses a farming image of fields needing rest to argue that renewal is part of growth. The essay ends with reflection questions for the reader.
points: Original intention is easy to lose once responsibilities and expectations accumulate.
How leaders choose to lead matters as much as what they intend to accomplish.
Carrying habits of urgency into new work risks reproducing the old patterns.
Rest and renewal are presented as part of growth, as with fields left fallow.
A more humane pace allows listening, reflection and alignment with one's purpose.
quotes: That original intention may be among the most important things they carry into office, and one of the easiest to lose sight of once they arrive.

Responsibilities increase, expectations accumulate, and we become increasingly occupied with meeting the demands of the roles we have assumed. Sometimes we become so accomplished at doing what is expected that we lose our connection to what inspired us in the first place.
If we truly want different outcomes from the people elected last week, part of the change must come through how they choose to lead, as well as what they intend to accomplish.
Otherwise, we risk carrying familiar habits of urgency, pressure, and constant activity into the very new experiences we are trying to create.
Fields that are continually worked without time to replenish eventually lose their vitality. Periods of rest allow the soil to recover and prepare for what it will nourish next.
Perhaps one of the most consequential changes we could make is to establish a more humane pace for how we live and lead.
Imagine them consciously establishing a way of working that allows room for reflection, genuine relationships, and the wisdom of those whose experiences differ from their own.
